title: 6. Other Column Models
intro: HTM and the Thousand Brains Theory are one answer to what a cortical column computes. This section covers the other main answers and the most-used simulation models: Douglas and Martin's canonical microcircuit, predictive coding, the Potjans–Diesmann full-density spiking microcircuit, and the Blue Brain digital reconstruction — what each assumes, how detailed it is, and when to use it.

blocks.text: Why look beyond HTM and Thousand Brains

HTM and the Thousand Brains Theory (sections 4 and 5) give one detailed answer to the question 'what does a column compute?': it learns sequences and objects as features at locations, using sparse codes and dendritic prediction. That answer is not the consensus. Other influential traditions answer differently — the column amplifies and selects (canonical microcircuit), the column computes prediction errors (predictive coding), or 'we should first build the column as faithfully as possible and then ask' (data-driven reconstruction). Knowing them helps in three ways: you can borrow their tested parts (connection tables, E/I populations, error units), you can benchmark against them, and you can position your own model honestly.

A useful mental axis runs from function-first to data-first. Function-first models (HTM, predictive coding) commit to a computation and keep only what it needs. Data-first models (Potjans–Diesmann, Blue Brain, the Allen V1 model) commit to anatomical and physiological realism and ask what activity emerges. The canonical microcircuit sits in the middle: a data-derived skeleton with a functional interpretation.

items: Canonical microcircuit (Douglas & Martin 1989, 1991, 2004). Assumes the column amplifies weak thalamic input by recurrent excitation and selects among inputs through inhibition (soft winner-take-all). Detail: three or four rate or spiking populations. Use it as the skeleton for any multi-layer column and to reason about gain and stability.

Predictive coding (Rao & Ballard 1999; Bastos et al. 2012; Keller & Mrsic-Flogel 2018). Assumes the column predicts its input and passes forward prediction errors; laminar mapping (errors superficial, predictions deep) is a hypothesis. Detail: abstract representation and error units, usually rate-based. Use it when you want a column that learns a generative model with local learning rules, or to explain mismatch responses.

HTM / Thousand Brains (sections 4 and 5, for comparison). Assumes the column learns sequences and object models in location-based reference frames, with prediction implemented as dendritic depolarisation. Detail: binary neurons with dendritic segments, minicolumns. Use it for online sequence learning and sensorimotor object recognition.

Potjans–Diesmann microcircuit (2014). Assumes nothing about function; asks whether layer- and cell-type-specific connectivity explains layer-specific activity. Detail: about 77,000 LIF neurons, 8 populations, about 0.3 billion synapses. Use it as a validation and benchmark network for simulators and hardware, and as a connectivity prior for your own column.

Blue Brain reconstruction (Markram et al. 2015). Assumes that a faithful enough reconstruction will reveal function through simulation. Detail: about 31,000 multi-compartment neurons, 55 m-types, 207 me-types, about 37 million synapses. Use it as a data source and for mechanistic in silico experiments, not as a starting point for a learning column.

Allen V1 model (Billeh et al. 2020). Data-driven model of mouse V1 with about 230,000 neurons, in biophysical and point-neuron (GLIF) versions, driven by a model of thalamic input. Use it when you want realistic cell types and visual responses in a model that is easier to run than Blue Brain.

Mean-field and neural-mass column models (Wilson & Cowan 1972; Jansen & Rit 1995). Describe each population by its average rate or potential. Detail: a few differential equations per column. Use them to analyse stability, oscillations and EEG-like signals, or to scale to many columns cheaply; they cannot represent sparse codes or individual spikes.
Canonical Microcircuit — Douglas and Martin's recurrent amplification circuit, the L4 → L2/3 → L5 → L6 flow and the Binzegger et al. synapse map; the conceptual base for everything else here.
Predictive Coding — Rao and Ballard's prediction-error hierarchy, precision weighting, the Bastos et al. laminar hypothesis, mismatch responses, and a direct comparison with HTM.
Potjans–Diesmann Microcircuit — the full-density 8-population LIF model: population sizes, connection table, parameters, emergent rates, how to run it and its role as a benchmark.
Blue Brain and Detailed Reconstruction — what the 2015 digital reconstruction contains, how it was built, what it showed, the critiques, and what to borrow from it.

blocks.text: Choosing a model for your project

items: You want a learning column on neuromorphic hardware: take the functional core from HTM or predictive coding, and the population structure and E/I ratios from the canonical microcircuit or Potjans–Diesmann.
You want to validate a new simulator, FPGA design or vector-based engine: run Potjans–Diesmann and compare per-population rates, irregularity and correlations with the reference implementation.
You want biologically grounded parameters (cell-type fractions, connection probabilities, short-term plasticity): look them up in Blue Brain, Allen and the Binzegger and Thomson datasets.
You want to understand dynamics (stability, oscillations, gain): reduce to a mean-field or rate model of the canonical circuit first, then return to spikes.
You want to compare theories: implement prediction-by-gating (HTM) and prediction-by-subtraction (predictive coding) on the same spiking substrate and run the same mismatch or sequence test.
The column models differ less in anatomy than in what they say the anatomy is for: amplification, error computation, sequence and object learning, or no stated function.
The canonical microcircuit's recurrent E/I loops are common ground; almost every spiking column model contains them.
Potjans–Diesmann is the de facto benchmark for spiking cortical simulation; reproducing it is a strong correctness check for your toolchain.
Laminar function assignments (errors in L2/3, predictions in L5/6; or HTM's layer roles) are hypotheses. Build them in deliberately, and label them as such.
More biological detail does not automatically mean more insight; choose the level of detail your question needs.
